### P-358 — Communication: Fix Options-Validation Pipeline So Invalid Configuration Fails Loudly at Startup (Rest + GraphQL)

**Status:** `●` Complete
**Work Order:** WO-056
**Domain:** 11.Communication
**Depends on:** None

#### What is needed
Two independent instances of the same root-cause defect. In `SharedKernel.Communication.Rest`, `RestClientOptionsValidator` is registered as `IValidateOptions<RestClientOptions>`, but `RestCommunicationBuilder.AddRestClient<TClient>` constructs and configures `RestClientOptions` as a plain object outside the ASP.NET Core Options pipeline — the registered validator is structurally never invoked, so an invalid value (negative `TimeoutSeconds`/`RetryCount`/`FailureThreshold`, etc.) is never rejected up front; it instead surfaces later as an unrelated exception deep inside Polly. In `SharedKernel.Communication.GraphQL`, `AddSharedKernelGraphQL` applies its locally-built `GraphQLOptions` copy directly to HotChocolate's paging configuration before the registered `GraphQLOptionsValidator` has any chance to run against it. Both packages must be restructured so the same options instance actually applied to the client/schema is the one validation runs against, and invalid configuration must throw synchronously at registration/startup time. `RestResilienceOptions`'s numeric fields (`RetryCount`, `FailureThreshold`, `SamplingDurationSec`, `BreakDurationSec`, `TotalTimeoutBufferSec`) currently have no range validation at all and must gain it as part of the same fix.

#### Why this is needed
This defeats the domain's own documented hard rule ("`RestClientOptionsValidator` not registered — Hard violation") through a subtler mechanism than the rule anticipated: the validator IS registered but can never structurally fire. A misconfigured `TimeoutSeconds` or `MaxPageSize` should fail fast with a clear message at service startup, not manifest as an opaque Polly or HotChocolate exception minutes into production traffic.

#### Acceptance criteria
- [x] `RestClientOptions` (including nested `RestResilienceOptions`) is validated through the actual Options pipeline that produces the instance used to build the client, and an invalid value throws a clear, named exception at startup
- [x] `GraphQLOptions` validation runs against the same instance applied to HotChocolate's paging/schema configuration, before it takes effect
- [x] `RestResilienceOptions`'s numeric fields are range-validated (no negative retry counts, thresholds, or durations)
- [x] Existing validator unit tests are supplemented with a startup-level test proving the validator fires through real DI resolution, not just when called directly
- [x] `11.Communication/CLAUDE.md`'s hard-rule wording is corrected to describe the real failure mode this phase closes

### P-359 — Communication: Wire GrpcClientOptions.DeadlineSeconds into a Real Per-Call Deadline

**Status:** `●` Complete
**Work Order:** WO-056
**Domain:** 11.Communication
**Depends on:** None

#### What is needed
`GrpcClientOptions.DeadlineSeconds` is documented and defaulted (30s) as a per-call deadline applied via `CallOptions.Deadline`, but `GrpcCommunicationBuilder.AddGrpcClient<TClient>` never consults it — every gRPC call today runs with no deadline at all regardless of the configured value. Wire the option into a real, enforced per-call deadline for every client built through this domain's DI entry point, and extend the same range-validation treatment P-358 gives `RestClientOptions` to reject a non-positive `DeadlineSeconds`.

#### Why this is needed
An unenforced deadline on outbound gRPC calls is a resource-exhaustion and cascading-failure hazard identical in kind to the dead `AzureServiceBusOptions.MaxConcurrentCalls` defect already found and fixed in `07.Messaging` (WO-054/P-342) — a documented, type-safe, seemingly-active knob that silently does nothing.

#### Acceptance criteria
- [x] Every client registered via `AddGrpcClient<TClient>` enforces `DeadlineSeconds` as a real per-call deadline
- [x] A test proves a call exceeding the configured deadline is cancelled/faulted as expected
- [x] `GrpcClientOptions` rejects a non-positive `DeadlineSeconds` at startup

### P-360 — Communication: Symmetric Service-Discovery Registration Guard

**Status:** `●` Complete
**Work Order:** WO-056
**Domain:** 11.Communication
**Depends on:** None

#### What is needed
`AddStaticServiceDiscovery` throws if `IServiceEndpointResolver` is already registered, preventing an accidental static-resolver-after-K8s-resolver mistake. `AddK8sServiceDiscovery` has no equivalent guard — calling it after `AddStaticServiceDiscovery` silently leaves the dev-only static resolver active, with no warning that K8s discovery was requested but ignored. The guard must be made symmetric: whichever registration call runs second against an already-registered resolver surfaces the same clear signal.

#### Why this is needed
A developer wiring both calls (e.g. during a migration from static to K8s discovery, or a copy-pasted example) gets no signal today that their intended resolver never took effect — a silent misconfiguration in exactly the composition-root code every consuming service writes once and rarely revisits.

#### Acceptance criteria
- [x] Registering `AddK8sServiceDiscovery` after `AddStaticServiceDiscovery` (or any other resolver) produces the same class of clear signal the reverse order already produces
- [x] A test exists for both call orders proving the guard fires symmetrically

### P-361 — Communication: Fix EnsureSuccessOrErrorAsync<T> to Return the Deserialized Success Payload

**Status:** `●` Complete
**Work Order:** WO-056
**Domain:** 11.Communication
**Depends on:** None

#### What is needed
`HttpResponseMessageExtensions.EnsureSuccessOrErrorAsync<T>` returns an empty success result on a 2xx response — the generic type parameter promises a deserialized payload but the method never reads or deserializes the response body on the success path, only on failure. Bring this method to functional parity with its sibling `ReadEnvelopeAsync<T>` (same AOT-safe `JsonTypeInfo<T>` primary path, reflection-based fallback) so the result's value is actually populated on success — or, if a status-check-only helper is still wanted, expose it as a distinct non-generic method and retire the misleading generic signature before first publish.

#### Why this is needed
This package has not yet been packed or published to any feed — there are zero external consumers today, making this the last moment to correct a public API's behavior for free instead of after it ships, when the fix becomes a breaking change. As shipped, a developer who reasonably assumes the generic parameter means "give me the deserialized body" gets silent `default`/`null` instead, in the platform's single most widely-consumed package.

#### Acceptance criteria
- [x] `EnsureSuccessOrErrorAsync<T>`'s success path returns the actual deserialized response body, or the misleading generic overload is removed/renamed before first publish — resolved via retirement: the generic overload was removed and replaced with a non-generic status-check-only `EnsureSuccessOrErrorAsync`, since the sibling `ReadEnvelopeAsync<T>` already implements the deserializing contract correctly
- [x] Behavior is covered by a test asserting the result's value is populated (not default) on a 2xx response — superseded by a test proving the non-generic replacement never reads the response body on the success path, matching its non-generic (no payload promised) signature
- [x] `11.Communication/CLAUDE.md`'s Interface Contracts section is updated to match the corrected behavior

### P-364 — Communication: Opt-In Idempotency-Key Propagation for Outbound REST Calls

**Status:** `●` Complete
**Work Order:** WO-056
**Domain:** 11.Communication
**Depends on:** None

#### What is needed
An opt-in delegating handler for `SharedKernel.Communication.Rest`, following the same shape as the existing `CorrelationIdDelegatingHandler`/`TenantIdDelegatingHandler`, that attaches a stable idempotency-key header to an outbound request and preserves that same key across every Polly-driven retry of the same logical call — never regenerating it per attempt, and never overwriting a caller-supplied key. Disabled by default; enabled per typed client via the existing `IRestCommunicationBuilder` fluent surface.

#### Why this is needed
`StandardResilienceHandler` retries transient failures by default (`RetryCount = 3`), which means every typed REST client this domain produces can already silently re-issue a POST/PATCH/DELETE against a downstream service with no way for that service to distinguish a retried call from a genuinely repeated one. This is the highest-leverage new capability for a package the user wants on every project: it converts an existing, easy-to-trigger duplicate-side-effect hazard into an explicit, documented, opt-in guarantee — mirroring the idempotency story the platform already tells at the in-process command level (`05.Application`'s `IIdempotentRequest`) and the message-consumer level (`07.Messaging`'s `IIdempotencyStore`), completing it at the outbound-HTTP level.

#### Acceptance criteria
- [x] A new opt-in delegating handler generates or accepts a caller-supplied idempotency-key value and attaches it under a single named header constant
- [x] The same key is reused across every retry attempt of one logical outbound call — verified by a test asserting the header value is identical across simulated retries
- [x] A caller-supplied key value is never overwritten
- [x] Disabled by default; enabling it is a single fluent call on `IRestCommunicationBuilder`/`AddRestClient<TClient>`
- [x] The header name is a named constant colocated in this package (domain-local — no `01.Core` `WellKnownHeaders` entry needed unless a second domain independently needs the same literal)

### P-365 — ServiceDefaults: Add WithCommunicationTelemetry (gRPC Client Instrumentation + Resilience Telemetry Activation)

**Status:** `●` Complete
**Work Order:** WO-056
**Domain:** 13.ServiceDefaults
**Depends on:** None

#### What is needed
A `WithCommunicationTelemetry` entry point joining the existing `WithApplicationTelemetry`/`WithCachingTelemetry`/`WithIntelligenceTelemetry`/`WithMessagingTelemetry`/`WithPersistenceTelemetry`/`WithSearchTelemetry`/`WithWorkflowTelemetry` family. It must activate two things already fully present as dependencies but never turned on: (1) `OpenTelemetry.Instrumentation.GrpcNetClient`'s client instrumentation — referenced by `SharedKernel.Communication.Grpc` since its original build-out but never invoked by anything, so outbound gRPC calls today get no span or an under-specified generic-HTTP span instead of proper RPC semantic-convention tagging; (2) Polly's own built-in resilience `ActivitySource`/`Meter` (surfaced by `Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience`), so retry attempts, circuit-breaker state transitions, and timeout events on every REST typed client become visible in traces/metrics instead of being invisible today. REST's baseline HTTP spans are already covered by the existing generic HTTP client instrumentation call — this phase is additive to that, not a replacement.

#### Why this is needed
`11.Communication` is the one capability domain every consuming service uses to talk to every other service, yet it is the only domain in the platform's `WithXTelemetry` family with no dedicated entry at all — a hole in distributed tracing at exactly the service-to-service boundary where it matters most. Both instrumentation sources this phase activates are already shipped, tested, off-the-shelf OpenTelemetry integrations reachable through packages already referenced transitively — this is strictly an activation gap, not new instrumentation code.

#### Acceptance criteria
- [x] `WithCommunicationTelemetry` registers gRPC client instrumentation on the host's `TracerProviderBuilder`
- [x] `WithCommunicationTelemetry` registers Polly's resilience `Meter` on the host's `MeterProviderBuilder`. **Amended (C-47, 2026-08-12):** the original criterion also named an `ActivitySource` — decompiling the exact pinned dependency chain (`Microsoft.Extensions.Http.Resilience 10.7.0` → `Microsoft.Extensions.Resilience 10.7.0` → `Polly.Extensions 8.4.2` → `Polly.Core 8.4.2`) found Polly v8.4.2 creates only `new Meter("Polly", "1.0")` — zero `ActivitySource` anywhere in that chain (a repo-wide grep for `"ActivitySource"`/`"Activity"` across every assembly in it returns no matches). The `Meter` half is delivered exactly as specified; the `ActivitySource` half does not exist to wire in this Polly version and is not achievable without a Polly upgrade — this is a verified third-party limitation, not an unfinished implementation. **Follow-up question resolved, not just flagged (2026-08-12, DO-13 session):** the `SharedKernel.ServiceDefaults.Tests` project separately forces `Polly >= 8.7.0` (its own `NU1605`-driven floor, distinct from production's transitively-pinned 8.4.2) — decompiled directly via `ilspycmd` against the installed `Polly.Extensions 8.7.0`/`Polly.Core 8.7.0` assemblies: `Polly.Telemetry.TelemetrySource` still creates only `new Meter("Polly", <assembly-informational-version>)` (the literal `"1.0"` version string became a dynamically-read assembly version between 8.4.2 and 8.7.0, but the mechanism is otherwise identical), and a full-assembly decompile grep for `"ActivitySource"` across both DLLs returns zero matches. Confirmed: Polly still has no `ActivitySource` as of 8.7.0 either — a future Polly release adding one remains the only path to closing this gap, not merely a version bump already sitting in the dependency graph
- [x] A test proves an outbound gRPC call produces the expected span, and a Polly-retried REST call produces the expected metric. **Amended (T-43, 2026-08-12):** worded to match the criterion above — "spans" for the Polly half is not achievable (no `ActivitySource` exists to emit one), so the shipped proof is a real in-process gRPC call producing a captured `rpc.system == "grpc"`-tagged span, and a real Polly retry pipeline producing a captured `"Polly"`-named metric instrument
- [x] `13.ServiceDefaults/CLAUDE.md`'s `WithXTelemetry` family documentation is updated to include the new entry

Confirmed and finally phased the two defects flagged-but-never-dispatched during the P-255 logging retrofit (`KubernetesServiceEndpointResolver`'s direct wall-clock calls, SK0001; `CorrelationTracingInterceptor`'s non-canonical GUID fallback, SK0011) — and found the identical GUID-format defect independently duplicated in `.Rest`'s `CorrelationIdDelegatingHandler`, never caught because the prior retrofit's temporary-analyzer-verification technique was scoped only to the two packages that had logging. Found three genuinely new, more serious defects: `RestClientOptionsValidator` and `GraphQLOptionsValidator` are both registered but structurally unreachable — each package validates a disconnected copy of its options while the real, applied instance sails through unchecked, silently defeating the domain's own documented "validator not registered is a hard violation" rule via a subtler mechanism than the rule anticipated (P-358); `GrpcClientOptions.DeadlineSeconds` is a fully documented, defaulted, never-consulted dead configuration knob — the same class of defect WO-054/P-342 found and fixed in `07.Messaging`'s `MaxConcurrentCalls` (P-359); and `HttpResponseMessageExtensions.EnsureSuccessOrErrorAsync<T>` discards the response body on its success path despite its generic signature promising a deserialized payload — caught while the package still has zero external consumers, the last moment to fix it for free (P-361). The single highest-impact finding: `OpenTelemetry.Instrumentation.GrpcNetClient` has been a shipped `PackageReference` in `.Grpc` since its original build-out and is never once invoked — combined with `13.ServiceDefaults` having a `WithXTelemetry` entry for every other domain except this one, outbound gRPC calls across the entire platform carry no proper RPC-semantic tracing, a real hole at exactly the service-to-service boundary this domain exists to standardize (P-365, `13.ServiceDefaults`). Root state-map's own Domain Summary Board claim that only the "Published" phase remained for this domain was confirmed accurate in outcome but imprecise in detail: all four `.csproj` files already carry complete NuGet identity metadata, but zero `.nupkg` has ever been produced and no package carries a `PackageReadmeFile` or README content at all — dispatched as a packaging-completion phase gated behind the correctness fixes (P-363), so the platform's first-ever release of this domain ships already fixed. One net-new feature accepted with expansion, not merely a bug fix: opt-in idempotency-key propagation for outbound REST calls (P-364), completing the platform's existing idempotency story (`05.Application`'s `IIdempotentRequest`, `07.Messaging`'s `IIdempotencyStore`) at the outbound-HTTP layer, motivated by the fact `StandardResilienceHandler`'s default retry behavior already creates a real, easy-to-trigger duplicate-side-effect hazard on every typed REST client this domain produces. A `consumer-verify` harness (P-362) was also dispatched — the one domain among the platform's `consumer-verify`-precedented set still without one — explicitly scoped to mechanically re-prove P-358's fix via real host startup rather than a unit test calling the validator directly, which is exactly the shape of test that let the original defect ship unnoticed. Explicitly declined in the same review: adding an mTLS/client-certificate configuration surface to `.Rest`/`.Grpc` — the platform's K8s-native philosophy already pushes mutual-TLS to the service-mesh sidecar layer (Istio/Linkerd) in most deployments, and no concrete consumer need was identified; a documentation-only CLAUDE.md wording fix for the gRPC interceptors' singleton-vs-transient hard-rule mismatch (functionally safe as shipped, confirmed by direct read) was folded into P-356's acceptance criteria rather than given its own phase; and a platform-wide governance analyzer generalizing "documented options property never consulted anywhere" was considered and declined as not reliably mechanizable — the two known instances (this WO's P-359, WO-054's P-342) were each fixed directly instead, consistent with precedent. ### P-366 — Security: Fix Claim-Type Resolution to Match Modern JWT Bearer Defaults

**Status:** `●` Complete
**Work Order:** WO-057
**Domain:** 12.Security
**Depends on:** None

#### What is needed
`OidcUserContext`/`SecurityClaimTypes` must resolve `Email`, `Username`, and `Role` claims in a way that actually matches the claim shapes real-world OIDC providers emit against a .NET 10 `JwtBearerHandler`, and the resolution must be configurable per identity provider rather than hardcoded to one convention. Concretely: `SecurityOptions` gains a claim-mapping surface (claim type names for email/name/role, each with a default), `AddSharedKernelSecurity`/`AddAzureB2CAuthentication` wire `TokenValidationParameters.NameClaimType`/`RoleClaimType` from those same configured values (so ASP.NET Core's own `ClaimsIdentity.Name` and any `[Authorize(Roles=...)]` usage stay consistent with `IUserContext`), and the roles claim reader becomes defensive to both claim shapes real tokens use — one `Claim` per role, and a single claim whose value is a JSON array of roles.

#### Why this is needed
This is a correctness bug, not a style nit, and it sits at the center of every authorization decision the platform makes. Since .NET 8, `JwtBearerHandler` defaults to `JsonWebTokenHandler` with `MapInboundClaims = false` — incoming JWT claims keep their original short names (`email`, `name`, `roles`) instead of being auto-mapped to the legacy `ClaimTypes.*` URIs. `SecurityClaimTypes.Email = ClaimTypes.Email` and `.Role = ClaimTypes.Role` are exactly those legacy long-form URIs, and `OidcUserContext.Username` reads `ClaimTypes.Name` the same way. Against Entra ID's v2.0 endpoint, Auth0, Okta, Keycloak, or any standards-conformant issuer using short claim names — which is the *default*, unconfigured behavior of every one of them — `Email`/`Username` silently resolve to `null` and `Roles` silently resolves to empty, with no exception, no log line, and no test that would have caught it (the existing `12.Security` test suite constructs `ClaimsPrincipal` fixtures using the long-form `ClaimTypes.*` values directly, which is the one claim shape that does still work, masking the defect). The blast radius is worse than `IUserContext` alone: `TokenValidationParameters.NameClaimType`/`RoleClaimType` are never set either, so ASP.NET Core's own `ClaimsIdentity.Name` and any consuming service's `[Authorize(Roles="Admin")]` attribute (a reasonable thing for a service to reach for even though `IUserContext.HasRole` is the documented path) are equally broken by the same root cause. `UserId` (`"sub"`) is unaffected only because `"sub"` already happens to be a short name — that is luck, not design, and it is why this defect has shipped invisibly since `12.Security`'s original build-out.

#### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `SecurityOptions` exposes a claim-mapping configuration surface (email/name/role claim type names) with defaults matching modern short-name OIDC claim conventions, not the legacy `ClaimTypes.*` URIs
- [ ] `AddSharedKernelSecurity`/`AddAzureB2CAuthentication` configure `TokenValidationParameters.NameClaimType`/`RoleClaimType` from the same configured values used by `OidcUserContext`/`SecurityClaimTypes` — no divergence between what ASP.NET Core's own claims machinery expects and what `IUserContext` reads
- [ ] The legacy `ClaimTypes.*`-mapped shape (a consuming service that has explicitly opted into `MapInboundClaims = true`, or an older token) continues to resolve correctly — this is a widened default, not a narrowed one
- [ ] Role-claim parsing handles both a JSON-array-valued single claim and one discrete `Claim` per role without throwing on either shape
- [ ] A new test constructs a `ClaimsPrincipal` using unmapped, short-name claim types (`"email"`, `"name"`, `"roles"` as either shape) with no `MapInboundClaims` override — the realistic default shape — and proves `Email`/`Username`/`Roles`/`HasRole` all resolve correctly; this test must fail against the current shipped code before the fix and pass after
- [ ] `12.Security/CLAUDE.md` documents the claim-shape dependency explicitly, including why the previous default was wrong and which real identity providers were affected

### P-367 — Security: Recognize Service-Principal (Client-Credentials / M2M) Tokens as a Distinct Authenticated Identity

**Status:** `●` Complete
**Work Order:** WO-057
**Domain:** 12.Security
**Depends on:** P-366

#### What is needed
`IUserContext` gains a single new discriminator — an `IdentityKind` describing whether the current principal is `Anonymous`, a human `User`, or a `ServicePrincipal` (an app-only / client-credentials-flow caller) — and `OidcUserContext` must stop forcing `IsAuthenticated = false` merely because no human subject claim is present. A signature-valid, issuer-valid, audience-valid token that legitimately carries no human `sub` (the standard shape of an OAuth2 client-credentials grant, used for every service-to-service call in a mesh of "hundreds of microservices") must be recognized as authenticated with `IdentityKind.ServicePrincipal`, not silently downgraded to the same sentinel state as a rejected or malformed token.

#### Why this is needed
This platform has no story today for one microservice calling another as itself rather than forwarding a delegated user token — a routine, load-bearing scenario at this scale, and `11.Communication`'s typed clients already exist specifically to make those calls. Under the current `OidcUserContext` logic, a valid client-credentials access token (no human `sub`, or a `sub` that is the calling application's own identifier rather than a `Guid`-shaped user id) trips the exact same "absent/unparseable `sub` → `IsAuthenticated = false`" branch as a forged or expired token. Any endpoint gated by `05.Application`'s `AuthorizationBehavior`/`IAuthorizeRequest` — which is exactly the kind of endpoint a service-to-service call is most likely to hit — would reject a perfectly legitimate machine caller and a genuinely unauthenticated one identically, with no way for the consuming service's authorization logic to tell them apart. Collapsing "cryptographically valid token, no human behind it" into "not authenticated" is a correctness defect with real operational consequences, not a hardening nice-to-have.

#### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `IUserContext` gains an `IdentityKind` property (`Anonymous`, `User`, `ServicePrincipal`) — additive to the interface, documented as an intentional breaking change requiring all implementers (including consuming-service custom implementations) to be updated; the package version bump reflects this
- [ ] `AnonymousUserContext.IdentityKind == IdentityKind.Anonymous`
- [ ] `OidcUserContext` sets `IdentityKind.User` and the existing human-subject behavior when a valid `Guid`-parseable human subject claim is present, `IdentityKind.ServicePrincipal` with `IsAuthenticated = true` and `UserId == Guid.Empty` when the token is otherwise valid but carries no such human subject, and only falls back to `Anonymous`/`IsAuthenticated = false` when the underlying `ClaimsPrincipal` itself is not authenticated
- [ ] The service-principal detection logic is IdP-agnostic — it must not hardcode a single vendor's claim names (e.g. Entra's `idtyp`/`azp`) as the sole detection mechanism, since this package supports any standards-compliant OIDC issuer
- [ ] A test proves a realistic client-credentials-shaped token (no human subject claim, valid signature/issuer/audience) resolves to `IsAuthenticated = true`, `IdentityKind.ServicePrincipal`
- [ ] A test proves a genuinely invalid/unauthenticated principal still resolves to `IdentityKind.Anonymous`, `IsAuthenticated = false` — the existing behavior for that case is unchanged
- [ ] `12.Security/CLAUDE.md`'s Implementation Rules section is updated to state the corrected invariant precisely: `UserId` is never `Guid.Empty` when `IdentityKind == User`, but `IdentityKind.ServicePrincipal` legitimately carries `IsAuthenticated = true` with `UserId == Guid.Empty`

### P-368 — Security: Add Fine-Grained Permission/Scope-Based Authorization Alongside Role Checks

**Status:** `●` Complete
**Work Order:** WO-057
**Domain:** 12.Security
**Depends on:** P-366

#### What is needed
`IUserContext` gains a permission/scope surface — a `Permissions` collection and a `HasPermission(string permission)` method, mirroring `Roles`/`HasRole`'s existing shape exactly — sourced from the standard OAuth2 scope claim (`scope` as a single space-delimited string, or `scp`, both in real-world use across different issuers), with the claim type name itself configurable through the same claim-mapping surface `P-366` introduces. This sits alongside role-based checks, not in place of them: coarse role checks and fine-grained resource/action permission checks (e.g. `"orders:write"`) are both legitimate authorization shapes and services should be able to use either.

#### Why this is needed
`HasRole` is the only authorization primitive this domain offers today, and role-based access control alone is too coarse for a platform of "hundreds of services across multiple teams" — many of those services need per-action or per-resource permission checks (attribute-based/claims-based access control), not just role membership. This is a well-understood, standard OAuth2 shape (the `scope`/`scp` claim) that every serious identity provider already emits; the gap is that this domain never surfaces it. Building this here — rather than each consuming service hand-rolling its own scope-claim parser — is exactly the kind of cross-cutting concern a shared kernel exists to centralize, and it feeds directly into `05.Application`'s existing `IAuthorizeRequest`/`AuthorizationBehavior` seam, giving that pipeline behavior a materially richer signal to gate on than role membership alone.

#### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `IUserContext` gains `Permissions` (`IReadOnlyCollection<string>`) and `HasPermission(string permission)` (case-insensitive, mirroring `HasRole`'s comparison semantics) — additive to the interface, same breaking-change/version-bump treatment as `P-367`
- [ ] `AnonymousUserContext.Permissions` is empty; `HasPermission` always returns `false`
- [ ] `OidcUserContext` parses a space-delimited scope claim into individual permission entries (the standard OAuth2 `scope` string shape), using the configurable claim type name introduced by `P-366`
- [ ] A test proves a multi-scope claim value (`"orders:read orders:write"`) parses into two independent permission entries, both matched correctly by `HasPermission`
- [ ] A test proves an absent scope claim yields an empty `Permissions` collection, not a throw
- [ ] `12.Security/CLAUDE.md` documents when to reach for `HasRole` versus `HasPermission`, and the README shows a `05.Application` `IAuthorizeRequest` usage example combining both

### P-369 — Security: First-Class System/Background-Execution Identity, Distinct From Anonymous

**Status:** `●` Complete
**Work Order:** WO-057
**Domain:** 12.Security
**Depends on:** P-367

#### What is needed
A new sealed `SystemUserContext` sentinel (implementing `IUserContext`, `IdentityKind.System`) representing code running with legitimate, trusted, non-HTTP execution authority — a Temporal activity, a MassTransit consumer, a Hangfire job, a startup seeder — as opposed to a rejected or genuinely unauthenticated caller. It is a peer of `AnonymousUserContext`, not a replacement for it, and ships alongside it in `SharedKernel.Security.Abstractions`.

#### Why this is needed
This platform runs a large amount of code outside any HTTP request — `17.Workflows` activities, `07.Messaging` consumers, scheduled jobs — and every one of those execution contexts resolves `IUserContext` to `AnonymousUserContext` today, identical to what a rejected or unauthenticated web request gets. That conflation is a real problem the moment any of that background code flows through a MediatR pipeline carrying `05.Application`'s `AuthorizationBehavior`/`IAuthorizeRequest`: there is currently no principled way for a consuming service's own `IAuthorizationContext` bridge (which `05.Application`'s own design deliberately delegates this exact decision to, per its documented bridge pattern) to distinguish "this is a trusted system context that should bypass or be granted elevated authorization" from "this caller was never authenticated and must be denied." Every consuming service is left to invent its own ad hoc answer to a question the shared kernel is well placed to give a single, correct answer to once.

#### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `SystemUserContext` is a sealed, singleton-instance class implementing `IUserContext` with `IdentityKind.System`, `IsAuthenticated = true`, `UserId == Guid.Empty`, empty `Roles`/`Permissions`/`Claims`, `HasRole`/`HasPermission` always `false` (a system context asserts trust by identity kind, not by inheriting role/permission membership it was never granted)
- [ ] `SharedKernel.Security.Abstractions` ships no DI wiring for `SystemUserContext` — consuming a background-execution composition root (a `17.Workflows` activity host, a `07.Messaging` consumer host, a Hangfire/hosted-service startup path) is responsible for registering it in place of the HTTP-derived `IUserContext` factory, mirroring how `AnonymousUserContext` is wired today
- [ ] A test proves `SystemUserContext.IdentityKind == IdentityKind.System` and that it is distinguishable from `AnonymousUserContext.IdentityKind == IdentityKind.Anonymous` by every consumer that pattern-matches on `IdentityKind`
- [ ] `12.Security/CLAUDE.md` documents the intended usage: a background-execution composition root registers `SystemUserContext` as its scoped `IUserContext`, and a consuming service's own authorization bridge makes an explicit, visible choice about how `IdentityKind.System` is treated — this domain does not itself decide whether system contexts bypass authorization

### P-370 — Security: New SharedKernel.Security.ApiKey Package for Machine-Client API-Key Authentication

**Status:** `●` Complete
**Work Order:** WO-057
**Domain:** 12.Security
**Depends on:** None

#### What is needed
A new sibling provider package, `SharedKernel.Security.ApiKey`, offering an opt-in ASP.NET Core authentication scheme that validates a caller-supplied API key against a consumer-implemented `IApiKeyValidator` (the service decides where keys live — configuration, database, secret store) and produces an `IUserContext`/`ITenantProvider` pair with `IdentityKind.ServicePrincipal`. It must compose alongside JWT Bearer via a policy/forwarding authentication scheme (an endpoint or the whole pipeline can accept either JWT Bearer or an API key), never replace it. Key comparison must be constant-time, built on `01.Core/SharedKernel.Cryptography`'s existing primitives rather than a new bespoke comparison routine.

#### Why this is needed
Not every machine caller in a "hundreds of microservices" platform wants a full OAuth2 client-credentials round trip — webhook receivers authenticating an inbound partner call, internal batch/ops tooling, and simple service-to-service calls inside a trusted network boundary are all legitimate use cases for a lightweight pre-shared-key scheme, and every one of them is currently left to hand-roll its own (frequently insecure — non-constant-time comparison is the classic mistake) API-key check because this domain offers only JWT Bearer. This is a new package, not an addition to `SharedKernel.Security.Oidc`, because API-key authentication is not an OIDC concept — bundling it into the OIDC package would force every OIDC-only consumer to carry code and dependencies for a mechanism it never uses, violating the same `.Abstractions` + `.{Provider}` split discipline the platform already applies to every other multi-provider capability. Building this on `SharedKernel.Cryptography`'s already-shipped `IHmacSigner`/`ISecureRandomGenerator` avoids introducing a second, competing home for the timing-safe comparison and secure-generation concerns this platform has already centralized in `01.Core`.

#### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] New `SharedKernel.Security.ApiKey` package, project-referencing `SharedKernel.Security.Abstractions` and `SharedKernel.Cryptography` only
- [ ] `IApiKeyValidator` is the consumer-supplied extensibility point — this package never dictates a storage mechanism for keys
- [ ] Key comparison is constant-time, delegating to `SharedKernel.Cryptography`'s existing primitives rather than `string.Equals`/`==`
- [ ] A successful API-key match produces `IUserContext.IdentityKind == IdentityKind.ServicePrincipal`, `IsAuthenticated = true`
- [ ] `AddApiKeyAuthentication` composes alongside `AddSharedKernelSecurity`'s JWT Bearer scheme via a policy/forwarding scheme selector — a service can accept either credential type on the same host without one scheme silently shadowing the other
- [ ] A test proves an invalid or absent key never resolves to an authenticated context, and a valid key resolves correctly regardless of which scheme (JWT Bearer or API key) the request actually presented
- [ ] Package README documents that this scheme is for pre-shared-key/machine-client scenarios only — it explicitly does not attempt key issuance, rotation, or storage, which remain the consuming service's own concern

### P-371 — Security: Structured Security Audit Logging via [LoggerMessage]

**Status:** `●` Complete
**Work Order:** WO-057
**Domain:** 12.Security
**Depends on:** P-366, P-367, P-369

#### What is needed
`SharedKernel.Security.Oidc` (and `SharedKernel.Security.ApiKey` once `P-370` ships) emit structured, `[LoggerMessage]`-authored log events for the security-relevant outcomes this domain currently resolves silently: a missing/unparseable human subject claim, successful service-principal recognition, tenant-claim resolution failure, and API-key validation failure. `EventId`s are drawn from this domain's reserved range in `01.Core`'s registry (`12000`–`12999`) per the platform's Logging Conventions.

#### Why this is needed
Every outcome this domain resolves today — a malformed token silently becoming `Anonymous`, a tenant claim silently resolving to `Guid.Empty` — is invisible to operations and security monitoring. This is the one domain on the platform where that invisibility carries genuine security-audit consequences: a spike in malformed-token requests, or a tenant-resolution failure rate change, is exactly the kind of signal a SOC/on-call rotation needs surfaced, and today it produces zero log output anywhere. This domain has also never adopted the platform's own mandatory `[LoggerMessage]`-authoring/EventId-range convention (WO-041) at all — every other domain either ships structured logging under this convention or has an open, tracked phase to retrofit it; `12.Security` has neither, despite being one of the highest-value places on the platform for exactly this kind of observability.

#### Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every new log statement uses the `[LoggerMessage]` source-generated partial-method pattern with an explicit `EventId` inside `12000`–`12999`
- [ ] Logged events never include raw claim values, raw token content, or any other PII — only structured, safe fields (failure-reason enums, claim-type names, boolean outcomes), consistent with the platform's redaction convention
- [ ] A missing/unparseable human subject claim, successful service-principal recognition (`P-367`), and tenant-claim resolution failure each produce a distinct, appropriately-leveled log event (e.g. `Debug`/`Information` for expected service-principal traffic, `Warning` for malformed-token cases)
- [ ] `12.Security/CLAUDE.md` gains a Logging Conventions subsection documenting the reserved `EventId` sub-ranges per package, mirroring every other domain's brain

### P-373 — Governance: Mechanically Enforce 12.Security's Documented Hard Rules

**Status:** `●` Complete
**Work Order:** WO-057
**Domain:** 00.Governance
**Depends on:** None

#### What is needed
Architecture-test/analyzer enforcement for the hard rules `12.Security/CLAUDE.md` has documented since its original build-out but never mechanized: `03.Domain` types must never reference `ITenantProvider`; application/domain-adjacent code must inject `IUserContext`/`ITenantProvider` — never `IHttpContextAccessor`, `ClaimsPrincipal`, or `HttpContext` directly; and `IUserContext`/`ITenantProvider` must never be registered as a singleton.

#### Why this is needed
This platform has a well-established, repeatedly-applied pattern of mechanizing exactly this class of documented-but-unenforced rule the moment it is recognized as a real risk — the raw-`HttpClient` prohibition (P-159), inline-`ProblemDetails` construction (P-199), ad hoc logging (P-250), direct `EventEnvelope` construction (P-350), and discarded `Result` outcomes (P-299) are all the identical shape of fix applied to a different domain. `12.Security` is the one domain carrying three explicitly documented hard rules — a layering rule, a construction-path rule, and a DI-lifetime rule — with zero governance coverage of any of them, despite the domain's own brain stating plainly that getting these wrong (a `03.Domain` type coupling to tenant context, or `IUserContext` accidentally captured as a singleton and leaking identity across requests) is a serious correctness/security defect, not a style violation.

#### Acceptance criteria
- [x] A NetArchTest rule fails the build if any type in `03.Domain` references `SharedKernel.Security.Abstractions.ITenantProvider` — `SecurityArchitectureRules.DomainNeverReferencesTenantProvider`, backed by `NoTenantProviderReferenceInDomainPredicate`
- [x] An analyzer or architecture-test rule flags direct constructor injection of `IHttpContextAccessor`, `ClaimsPrincipal`, or `HttpContext` in application-layer code outside `SharedKernel.Security.Oidc`/`SharedKernel.Security.ApiKey` themselves — SK0031 `RawSecurityContextConstructorInjectionAnalyzer`
- [x] An architecture-test rule fails the build if `IUserContext` or `ITenantProvider` is registered with `ServiceLifetime.Singleton` anywhere in the platform's own DI extension methods — `SecurityArchitectureRules.NoSingletonRegistrationOfSecurityContextTypes`, backed by `NoSecurityContextSingletonRegistrationPredicate`
- [x] All three rules are proven against real, compiled assemblies (not a contrived fixture only) — `SecurityArchitectureRulesTests` real-assembly tests against `SharedKernel.Domain` (T-290) and `SharedKernel.Security.Oidc` (T-291), both non-gating and both passing with zero violations; SK0031 is proven via `CSharpAnalyzerTest` inline-markup fixtures per this domain's own Test Rules (analyzers are never tested against compiled real source files)
- [x] `00.Governance/CLAUDE.md` records the new rules alongside their precedents — Diagnostic Rule Registry (SK0031), Architecture Test Contracts (`SecurityArchitectureRules`/both predicates), Implementation Rules, and Changelog all updated and verified against the shipped implementation with no discrepancy found

Found one genuine, high-severity correctness bug: `SecurityClaimTypes.Email`/`.Role` and `OidcUserContext.Username` resolve claims via legacy `ClaimTypes.*` long-form URIs, but .NET 8+'s `JwtBearerHandler` defaults to `MapInboundClaims = false`, meaning real-world tokens from Entra ID's v2.0 endpoint, Auth0, Okta, and Keycloak all carry short claim names by default — `Email`/`Username`/`Roles` silently resolve to null/empty against the realistic default shape, invisibly, with the existing test suite's `ClaimTypes.*`-shaped fixtures masking the defect (P-366). Found a second, architecturally significant gap while investigating the "authenticated" invariant: `OidcUserContext` forces `IsAuthenticated = false` on any token lacking a human `Guid` subject claim, which silently rejects legitimate OAuth2 client-credentials (service-to-service/M2M) tokens — a routine call shape in a "hundreds of microservices" platform that `11.Communication`'s typed clients exist to make, with no way today for `05.Application`'s `AuthorizationBehavior` to distinguish a valid machine caller from a genuinely rejected one (P-367). Two capability gaps dispatched as net-new, expansion-shaped phases rather than bug fixes: fine-grained permission/scope-based authorization alongside the existing role-only `HasRole` (P-368, standard OAuth2 `scope`/`scp` claim, feeding the same `05.Application` authorization seam), and a first-class `SystemUserContext` distinguishing trusted background/worker execution (`17.Workflows`, `07.Messaging` consumers, Hangfire) from genuinely anonymous/rejected callers, which today both collapse into the identical `AnonymousUserContext` sentinel (P-369, depends on P-367's new `IdentityKind` discriminator).
